Explore / Where can people and firms actually reach financial services — and where is the map still blank?

Access: where services can be reached is only partly mapped

Parts of the access picture are documented: the provider lists of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), its reported total of 1,473 POS terminals in January 2026 within its reporting scope, dated status decisions, and a 2016–2019 study showing e-money accounts concentrated in cities. The evidence does not yet establish, consistently across Yemen, which access points are operating at a particular place and date.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
How numbers are presented

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

What a roster or infrastructure count cannot establish

A licence or roster entry does not prove current operation at every named location. A system-level count of terminals or service points does not establish where people can reach a service. Missing geography is unknown, not zero, and spatial overlap with electricity, connectivity, population or conflict does not by itself establish causality.

Why this resource does not show a complete map now

A missing location record is not evidence that no service exists. Where operation cannot be verified, this resource shows the location as not observed or not currently evidenced. It does not turn an unobserved point into zero, or a licence, branch name or historical provider study into current operating presence.

01
Evidence

What official lists and payment reports can show

Official rosters and decisions can establish listing, licensing or a dated status event. Payment reports issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) can establish system totals within that bank’s reporting scope for specified dates; how far that scope covers each area of Yemen is not established. These are useful pieces of the access picture, but they are not a verified, geocoded network of operating service points.

02
Evidence

Lists show who is registered, not where services operate

Official lists document a substantial exchange and remittance provider presence relevant to the access question. The 2026 roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents — three source categories, not a deduplicated count of firms — and the CBY-Aden list of licensed banks, as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks. Listing or licensing is not operation. The 2026 suspension, withdrawal or closure decisions are separate status events: they are dated January–September 2026, some were issued before the roster and some after it, and the roster’s own issue date is not stated. Separately, the results framework of the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) sets a January 2025 baseline of 817 financial access points against a 2030 target of 1,021, under a project definition that the evidence base does not document. None of these figures shows where services operate or how far people are from them.

03
Analysis

Infrastructure can expand without telling us who can reach it

POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026, within that bank’s reporting scope. This establishes a change in the reported terminal stock. It does not show where every terminal is located, how many merchants or unique users it represents, whether the terminals are active, or how evenly access is distributed.

Another view of the evidence

What is observed — and what is still unmapped

Text description of this view
  1. Analytical question: Which access locations are verified, and where is geography still unknown?
  2. What the evidence shows: The evidence base does not yet establish, consistently across Yemen, which access points operate at a given place and date: it holds no verified, dated register of operating locations. What it holds are official lists, dated status events for providers, payment-infrastructure totals and historical studies of where providers were concentrated; none of these records where services operate on a given date. A location would appear as a point only with a verified source, an observation date, a dated operating status and a permitted level of geographic detail. Places with no observed location are unknown, not zero, and a listed or licensed provider does not by itself establish an operating service point.
  3. Scope and time: Specific to each item · Only observed and source-dated locations in the evidence register
  4. What not to conclude: An area with no observed location is not an area without access, and a listing or licence does not show an operating service point.
04
Measurement

What a reliable national access atlas would require

For each service point, a reliable access atlas would require — subject to safety and rights — the permitted location or geographic level, channel type, operator, operating status, last verification date, available services, and any restriction on publication or spatial precision. Population, travel time, connectivity and conflict/access constraints could then be added as separate dated layers.

Analysis

Historical provider evidence shows concentration, not a map of access after 2019

A five-provider study covering 2016–2019 reports that e-money accounts/users were concentrated in cities at an average 93.8%, while women represented about 13% on average. It reports 807,919 e-money accounts in December 2019 and an average dormant/inactive share of 23%. These are historical observations for the providers the study covered. They are useful for showing why account counts cannot be read as active people or current geographic access; they are not national prevalence or a present-day access map.

System context

Where access sits in the wider system

Access sits between the presence of providers or infrastructure and actual use. Understanding it requires evidence on provider authority and operating status, reachable geography, channel and service type, followed separately by evidence on whether people or firms actually use the service and the quality they experience.

Evidence Readings on this question

Evidence Reading

When the unit changes, the story changes

People, accounts, subscribers, terminals and transactions all describe parts of Yemen’s financial system. They are not interchangeable measures of financial inclusion, and a target or a trend is only as sound as the unit it keeps.

What measurement would change the decision?

A register of active financial access points

An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.

This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.
Open this measurement priority

Reform transmission and service quality

Reform-specific operational and user-side evidence tied to the same implementation timeline, from go-live through coverage, reliability, cost and outcome.

This evidence would show the furthest evidenced state of each reform and the next unmeasured result without treating missing evidence as failure.
